header.title: Huon de Bordeaux (G): AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Anonymous
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's urn:geste:ed-huong:dipl, from the Geste corpus of chansons de geste, Camps et al. (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. Only some passages are translated so far: those that the Atlas of Ancient Myth, Magic in the Ancient Texts and the demons-and-angels study cite.
header.statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
header.availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit the Geste corpus of chansons de geste, Camps et al. and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

notes.3644: 3655: 'enviré' is uncertain: he circled it, or turned it, three times. 3719: '. cm .' read as a hundred thousand. 3722: 'si cier que t'as de m'amor desevrer' is unclear; taken as an appeal to how much Huon would hate to lose Oberon's love. 3727: 'tu te pues bien vanter', literally 'you may well boast', taken as 'you may be sure'.
notes.10353: 10357, 10362: 'souhaide' (I wish) is Oberon's way of bringing things about by wishing them. 10393: 'j'oi' is supplied by the edition. 10406: the subject is unstated; probably God, possibly Huon.
notes.4: Line 10: the text reads '10Qui'; the '10' is a line number run into the text and is not translated.
notes.3492: 3497: the text reads 'lui conçus', taken as 'fui conçus' (I was conceived).
notes.3607: 3609: 'Li arc d'Amors' taken as the bows of Love worked into the chair; 'arc' could also mean arches.
notes.4923: 4925: the edition brackets 'quant il doit ajorner' with a stray 'b' before it, perhaps a siglum or marker. 'Le jor li traient', literally 'they draw the day for him', is uncertain; probably they sing in the dawn.
notes.2318: 2329 parjurés, literally 'forsworn': the sense seems to be that Huon will no longer stand as an oath-breaker toward Charlemagne. Charlemagne moves between tu and vous in this speech; English 'you' does not show it.
notes.5529: 5537 'Dont pert le voie': pert is taken from perdre, 'loses'; it could be from paroir, giving 'then the road to the palace appears'. 5549 S'est read as C'est.
notes.3159: 3171 esperés is doubtful: taken as 'roused, stirred' (esperir); it might mean 'filled with hope' or 'bewildered'. 3186 and 3192: the bracketed restorations begin with a stray 'b' from the transcription ([ben soi taire], [bsont plus aresté]), read as [en soi taire] and [sont plus aresté].
notes.4561: 4564 and 4566: the men are of copper; 'Tout sont de fer' seems to refer to the flails. 4567 'y ver' read as iver, 'winter'. 4573 Orgilleus means 'the Proud One'.
notes.5053: 5057 kavece: the neck-opening (chevece) of the hauberk. 5065 Avoir read as Avoit, 'had'. 5074 'je le n'ai esprové': odd word order, read as 'I have not tried it'.
notes.10193: 10200 Geramme (Gerame in the context) is a spelling of Geriaume. 10198 Li rois is taken as Oberon. 10222 crimineus agrees with an unstated pecié, 'sin', supplied in brackets.
notes.8994: 9002 li desvés, 'the mad, the raging', is an epithet of Gerard (Gerars, Girars); its exact force here is unclear.
notes.3331: 3343 'tu ne dis mie asés', literally 'you do not say enough', taken in its idiomatic sense 'you speak amiss'.
notes.5344: 5350 luiton: a sprite or goblin (lutin); Malabron takes on a sea creature's skin to carry Huon (5360, 5364). 5351 Huelins is a diminutive of Huon, rendered 'young Huon'. 5362-5363 read as 'cross yourself ... so that God may lead us', with 'ne poras mescaver' as an aside.

nodes.text: of Charlemagne of the steadfast heart,
and of Huon, who had such great valour,
and of Oberon, the little wild king,
who spent all his days living in the woods.
This Oberon, who had such great lordship,
know that he was the son of Julius Caesar,
who held Hungary, a wild land,
and Austria and all that inheritance.
He held Constantinople all his life;
he had seven great leagues of wall built,
which still stand as far as the wild sea.
Julius had as his wife a very wise lady,
Morgan was her name, she had a very fair face;
she was the mother of Oberon the wild,
and she had no other heir in all her life.
Now you shall hear a song of proud baronial deeds.
Lords, listen, and may God help you!
Be at peace, and leave off your noise;
and you will hear a song well worth praising,
of Charlemagne, who has France in his keeping,
and of Huon, the noble warrior,
who held Bordeaux and the great inheritance,
and of Oberon, the noble knight;
standing upright he was no more than three feet tall,
and he was enchanted, know it for truth.
It was at Pentecost, the high, great feast day,
that Charles of the fierce face held his court at Paris.
Than to go into hell to speak with the devils;
For you will have to go to such a place
If you want to be reconciled with me.
I have sent fifteen messengers there,
And I never saw a single one of them come back.
It is straight across the Red Sea,
In Babylon, the wondrous city.
There you must carry my message;
You will have to speak to King Gaudisse.
If you can do what you will hear me tell,
And can ever return to France again,
You will not be [held] forsworn toward me.
When you are across the Red Sea
And you come into the good city,
You must both pledge and swear
That you will wait to enter the palace
Until the emir is seated at dinner.
And after that you will go up into the palace
In just the way you will hear me tell you:
Hauberk on, jewelled helmet laced,
You will have to carry the naked sword,
And the first man you find at the meal,
He will never be so noble or so well connected
That you do not cut off his head at once.
And after that you will have to do something else:
Gaudisse the emir has a daughter,
That is Esclarmonde, who has such great beauty;
You must pledge and promise
That in sight of all you will kiss her three times,
And after that you will deliver my message
To the emir, in sight of all his barons.
On my behalf you will ask the emir
To send me a thousand moulted sparrowhawks,
A thousand bears, a thousand boarhounds well chained,
And a thousand squires, all young men,
And a thousand maidens of great beauty,
And from his beard the white grizzled whiskers,
And from his mouth four molar teeth.'
The French say: 'You want to kill him!'
'By God,' said Charles, 'you speak the truth!'
I knew nothing of it, so may God save me,
and then I saw my brother lying in the middle of the meadow;
know for truth, my heart was full of anger.
I went forward, my inscribed blade all bare;
why should I hide it, by God in majesty?
I killed Charlot, who was Charlemagne’s son.
I did not know at all that he had begotten him.
I went to court to defend myself;
but the body was brought there after me.
For he is more beautiful than the sun in summer.
He is called Oberon by his right name.
There is no living man, if he has entered the wood
And speaks to him, who can escape him;
And once he has stayed with him,
He will never leave there in all his life.
And I tell you, in all good faith,
That this dwarf has such great power
[That] when you think to pass through the woodland,
Before you have gone twelve leagues,
You will see him standing in front of you.
He will speak of God in majesty in such a way
That there is no man who would not be stirred by it.
If you will not speak to his noble person,
He will be so sorely vexed by it
That you will have very great fear in your heart,
For he will make it both rain and blow,
Make trees break and split violently apart.
And after he has worked in this way,
He will make for you a river so great
That one could take a great fleet on it,
And, to all appearance, a great sea-going ship.
But I tell you, know it for the truth,
All that you see there will be phantoms:
You will cross the water dry-footed;
You will wet neither hose nor shoe there.
I tell you plainly, you would be wrong to doubt it,
That [keeping silent] can do you no harm.
Take good care not to utter a single word;
For if you spoke, this is the plain truth,
You will never be free of him,
For by answering you have lost everything.'
'By my faith,' said Huon, 'I have no wish to speak there.'
Then they mount again and [stay there no longer],
if he shoots at it and it pleases him,
that he would not take it entirely at his will.
And he had at his neck a horn of bright ivory;
the horn was banded with bands of gold;
fairies made it on an island in the sea.
There was one of them who gave it a gift like this:
whoever hears the horn ring and sound,
if he is sick, at once returns to health,
however great an infirmity he may have.
And the next fairy gave it far better:
whoever hears the horn, this is the truth,
if he is starving, he is fully fed,
and if he is thirsty, he has drunk his fill.
And the next fairy gave it far better still:
that there is no man in such great hardship
that, if he hears the horn ring and sound,
he is not compelled to sing at the sound of the horn.
The fourth fairy chose to endow it better,
when she gave it such a gift as you shall hear:
that there is no march, nor land, nor kingdom,
as far as the Dry Tree, or beyond the sea,
if he wishes to make the horn ring and sound,
Oberon hears it at Monmur, his city.
The little man began to blow his horn,
and the fourteen begin to sing.
“Ah, God!” said Huon, “who is coming to visit us?
I feel no hunger nor any hardship.”
And Gériaume says: “It is the hunchbacked dwarf.
For God’s sake I beg you, sire, do not speak to him,
'By my faith,' said Huon, 'God has comforted us,
Since we have escaped from the dwarf like this.'
Old Geriaume spoke his mind about it:
'Sire,' he said, 'as God may save me,
You will very soon see the devil come back;
He will very soon come trotting up before you.'
While they were talking like this,
Just as they were about to cross a little bridge,
The little man leaps out in front of their noses.
Huon sees him and was much afraid.
'God!' said the youth, 'here is the devil again!'
Oberon hears him and spoke fiercely:
'Vassal,' he said, 'you do not speak rightly,
For, by Him who suffered on the cross,
I was never a fiend or a devil;
Rather I tell you truly, as God may save me,
I am a man of flesh like any other.
Again I come to conjure you in God's name,
By all that He has made and established,
By oil and chrism, by baptism and salt,
You do not know at all what man you have found;
you will know it, it will not be long.
Julius Caesar brought me up most tenderly;
Morgan the fairy, who had such great beauty,
she was my mother, so may God save me.
Of these two I was conceived and begotten;
they had no other heirs in all their lives.
At my birth there was great rejoicing;
they summoned all the barons of the kingdom;
fairies came there to visit my mother.
There was one of them who was not at all pleased,
and she gave me such a gift as you see,
that I would be a little hunchbacked dwarf;
and so I am, and I am grieved at heart by it.
I have not grown since I was three years old.
When she saw that she had made me like this,
she wished afterwards to amend her word for me;
and she gave me such a gift as you will hear,
that I would be the most handsome man of flesh
who ever was, after the Lord God.
Now I am such as you see me here;
I am as fair as the sun in summer.
And the other fairy gave me far better:
I know the heart and the thought of a man,
and I can tell how he has acted,
and besides that, his deadly sin.
The third fairy gave me far better,
to do more for me and to better me,
and she gave me such a gift as you will hear:
that there is no march, nor land, nor kingdom,
as far as the Dry Tree, or as far as one can travel,
where, if I wish myself there, in God’s name,
I would not be there, entirely at my will,
just as soon as I have said it,
with as many people as I wish to ask for.
And when I want to build a palace,
with many chambers and many great pillars,
I have it at once, you need not doubt it,
and such food as I wish to name,
and such drink as I wish to ask for.
And I was, truly, born right at Monmur;
it is far from here, I tell you in truth,
a full four hundred leagues can be counted to it:
I have gone there and come back more quickly
than a horse could cover an acre.”
Oberon said: “I was born at Monmur,
a city that belonged to my ancestor;
I have gone there and come back more quickly
than a horse could run across a little field.
On the faldstool sat the noble Oberon;
its feet were of fine refined gold,
the bows of Love were wrought on it.
Fairies made it on an island in the sea,
they had it presented to King Alexander,
who had tournaments made and established.
Afterwards he had it given to King Caesar;
he left it to his son out of love.
The faldstool was of such virtue
that if it falls into fire, it cannot burn;
whoever sits on it can be secure,
for he cannot be poisoned by anything,
by no venom can he be harmed:
at once he sees what has been brought to him,
by the power of the gilded faldstool.
The king had put on a *bliaut* [a long tunic],
which was all of natural silk,
Rather, I want to give you some of my treasures.”
At once he has called Gloriant:
“Brother,” he said, “bring me my cup.”
He goes to fetch it, and then has handed it to him,
and Oberon has grasped it in both hands.
“Huon,” he said, “look at this cup:
the great power that Jesus has given me
(in fairyland I do as I will),
you can now put it well to the test.
You see clearly now this good gilded cup,
which is quite empty, and soon it will be full.”
With his right hand he circled it three times,
then made over it the cross of God in majesty;
then it became full of wine and of spiced wine.
Oberon said: “Huon, now listen to me:
you have clearly seen how I have worked;
it is by God’s doing that this cup is such.
And it is moreover of such great virtue
that if all who are born of woman
and all the dead were raised to life again,
and had come here and gathered together,
this cup would give wine enough,
whatever drink one might wish to name,
provided a worthy man had it in his keeping;
for I tell you, in perfect good faith,
no one can drink from it unless he is a worthy man, by God,
and clean and pure and without mortal sin.
As soon as a wicked man tries to lay his hand on it,
he has lost the virtue of the cup.
So help me God, the king of majesty,
if you can drink from it, it will be given to you.”
“Sire,” said Huon, “may God reward you for it;
but I fear that I am not such a man
that I could either drink from it or touch it.
Never in my life have I seen such power;
to my mind, you know how to work enchantments.
Sire,” said Huon, “listen to me:
I tell you truly, I have confessed
to the pope in the city of Rome;
I repent of my mortal sins
in such a way, so may God save me,
that I hate no man born of woman.”
Then the noble young man steps forward;
he took the cup and grasped it in both hands,
put it to his mouth, for it was brimming with wine,
then drank from it in very great plenty.
When Oberon has seen all this,
he was very glad, and runs to embrace him:
“Huon, fair brother,” said the noble Oberon,
“so help me God, I have found you a worthy man;
now I give it to you, in the name of charity,
the good cup that has such virtue,
on such terms as you will now hear me say:
that if you take care, upon your loyalty,
to act in this by my counsel,
I will help you loyally, without fail;
but no sooner will you tell a lie
than you will lose the virtue of the cup
and all the friendship of my person.”
“Sire,” said Huon, “I believe I can guard well against that;
if you please, now let me go.”
Oberon said: “You will wait a little longer,
for I have in here a horn of bright ivory,
and since I have found you a worthy man,
and clean and pure and without mortal sin,
I will give it to you, as I hope for health;
you can very well carry it in your purse.
And besides this I want to pledge to you,
by the great power that Jesus has given me
in fairyland, where I have my dwelling:
you will never be in a kingdom so far away
that, if you blow this horn of bright ivory,
I will not hear it at Monmur, my city;
and I swear to you, upon my loyalty,
that I myself will be there ready,
with a hundred thousand armed men in my company,
for I will help you defend yourself against all men.
But one thing I want to command you,
as dearly as you would hate to be parted from my love,
and know it well in true faith:
I forbid you, on pain of having your limbs cut off,
ever to sound the horn for nothing;
for if you do it, so may God save me,
when you have no need, you may be sure
you will find yourself in such great misery
that there is no living man who would not take pity on it.”
“Sire,” said Huon, “I believe I can guard well against that;
now, if you please, let me go.”
There are twenty-five chambers in the ornamented palace;
No man ever heard tell of a richer one.
And there are two men at the entrance of the dwelling;
They are made and fashioned all of copper,
And each one holds a jointed flail;
They are all of iron, much to be feared.
They keep beating all the time, winter and summer,
And I tell you, in pure truth,
A lark, which knows how to fly very fast,
Could not fly into the palace
Without being killed; it could not escape.
And inside lives a great raging giant;
He is called Orgilleus by his right name.
there are four birds, much to be praised,
which sing all the time, winter and summer;
they herald the day for him [when it is about to dawn].
No harp or fiddle is so good to hear;
they were fashioned by necromancy.
Could never harm me in the slightest.
I took this dwelling from him, by my head,
And with it a good gilded hauberk.
There is no man born of a mother,
If he could get inside its neck-opening,
Who could ever be overcome by arms;
But it is not granted to everyone:
The writing that is on the collar says
That no one can put on the hauberk
Unless he is a worthy man and without mortal sin,
And clean and pure as if he were newly born.
And if the mother who bore him
Had ever in her life thought of a man
Other than the one who had married her,
Then he could not get into the hauberk.
And that is why I say the man is not born
Who could, by my head, put it on.
The hauberk is of such great worth
That he who has thrown it over his back,
If he falls into water, cannot sink,
If he falls into fire, cannot burn.
For, by Muhammad, I have not tried it on;
You gave me leave to arm myself,
By the faith I owe God, it is King Oberon.
'What!' said Huon, 'I do not know your name.'
'You shall know it: my name is Malabron;
I am of King Oberon's household;
So help me God, I am his liegeman.
My lord gave me such a gift
That I would be a sprite in the sea for thirty years.'
'Friend, fair brother,' said the valiant young Huon,
'For the love of God, who has all things to save,
Shall I dare to trust myself to your fair person?'
Said Malabron: 'You need not be afraid;
I will carry you across the Red Sea
Most faithfully and without any deceit,
In such a way, as God may save me,
That you will wet neither hose nor shoe.
But now be quick and get ready,
For I am going to get into my skin.
You will have to climb up on my back;
Cross yourself well (you cannot come to grief)
So that the true God may lead us to safety.'
Malabron has gone into his skin;
Huon has climbed onto his back,
And Malabron has leapt back into the sea.
I cannot tell you how long he took over the crossing,
But there is no servant or young man here
And if he comes, the devil will bring him.'
With that he fell silent and went on across.
The youth lamented to himself;
Then he said: 'The Lord God will help me.
I know for certain the devil bewitched me
When I lied at that bridge back there.'
Now Huon has crossed the four bridges.
When he was across and had set out on his way,
Then he loses the road to the great ornamented palace.
He has entered the emir's orchard;
God made no tree that could bear fruit
That he did not have planted in the orchard.
A spring runs there along its channel;
The stream comes from Paradise, without a lie.
There is no man born of a mother,
However old he may be, or white-haired or grizzled,
Who, if he can wash his hands in the stream,
Is not at once a lad and a young man [again].
Huon came there and stopped beside it;
He washed his hands and drank plenty of the water.
This is the spring of the emir Gaudisse;
The brook comes from the river of Paradise.
God made no woman, however much she has had her pleasure,
Who, if she drinks even a little of the water,
Is not a virgin as on the day she was born.
Huon was there, the young man of worth;
He washed his hands and sat down above it.
That spring, a serpent guarded it;
No wicked man will ever put his finger in it
Who is a traitor or false to his faith,
And if he comes there, he is dead on the spot.
Huon came there; the serpent bowed to him
By the power of the hauberk he was wearing;
He drank of the water and washed his white hands;
Now he forgot what he was supposed to do.
Huon was inside; he has entered the orchard.
At the spring of Gaudisse the emir
He left out nothing at all in the telling
that he could call to mind, great or small;
and the pope has forgiven him everything.
Afterwards he has wedded the maiden to him;
Mass was said, and, the service ended,
they come back into the adorned palace.
Then I took from him four molar teeth,
And after that, the white grizzled whiskers.'
Gerard said: 'Sire, and how do you keep them?'
'I will tell you,' said Huon, 'in God's name.
See Geriaume there, who has them in his side;
Above the hip he has them sealed in,
For Oberon the fairy put them there
By fairy power, by the will of God.'
'Which one is he?' said Gerard the madman.
And Huon replies: 'That old man you see there,
At once he freed all three of them from prison,
Then seated them beside him at dinner.
Oberon takes his good cup of bright gold,
And makes over it the cross of God in majesty,
And the cup became full of clear wine.
The king takes it and hands it to the lady.
And she drank, and handed it to Huon,
And he passes it to Geriaume the bearded.
And Oberon called to Huon:
'Quickly now,' he says, 'friend, get up,
And carry this good cup of bright gold
To Charlemagne, the mighty crowned king;
Give it to him to drink in the name of peace.
If he does not take it, so help me the Lord God,
I will make him pay dearly for it.'
Charles hears him, and did not know what to think;
He keeps quite still and silent, for he dares not speak
Because of the wonders he hears being worked.
'Sire,' said Huon, 'I will do all your will.'
Then he rose and took hold of the cup,
Came to Charles, and gave it to him.
The king takes it, for he dares not refuse it;
As soon as he held it, the wine was gone.
'Vassal,' said Charles, 'you have bewitched me.'
Said Oberon: 'No, your wickedness does it;
For the cup is of such worth
That no one can drink from it unless he is known as a worthy man,
And clean and pure and without mortal sin.
Rightful emperor, as God may save me,
I know of one [sin] that is very grievous,
Which you committed a very long time ago,
And you never confessed it to a priest;
If it were not that it would shame you,
I would tell it now without any delay.'
and give him half of my land.”
The French hear it, and weep for pity.
Oberon said: “So may God save me,
all the gold in the world could not reprieve them;
rather I wish them up there in the midst of the meadows,
so that all four of them may be dragged there,
by fairy power and by my dignity.
On a gallows let Gerard be hanged,
he and his lord, Gibouart of Viesmes,
and with them I wish there the abbot
and the other monk whom he had brought,
because they came to bear witness.
The gallows too I want to call up;
let them be higher than a bow can shoot.”
At once they were there, as he had described;
all four were hanged and dragged;
they have their reward for their great wickedness.
Charles sees it, and is greatly frightened by it,
then cried out, in the sight of all the barons:
“By my faith,” said Charles, “this man is the Lord God;
if he wished, we would all be killed.”
Oberon hears it, and has called out to him:
“Rightful emperor, so may God save me,
I am not God, but I am a man of flesh.
I am called Oberon by my right name;
right at Monmur, truly, there I was born.
Julius Caesar brought me up most tenderly,
he who had the roads built and laid out;
Morgan the fairy, who had such great beauty,
she was my mother, so may God save me;
nine full months she carried me within her.
At my birth there was great rejoicing;
they summoned all the great men of the kingdom.
Julius, my father, had a great feast proclaimed;
great was the court of high-born barons.
Fairies came there to visit my mother;
there was one of them who was not at all pleased,
and she gave me such a gift as you see,
that I would be a little hunchbacked dwarf;
and so I am, and I am grieved at heart by it:
I have not grown since [I had] passed three years.
When she saw that I was made like this,
she wished to amend her word somewhat,
and gave me such a gift as you see,
that I would be the most handsome man of flesh
who ever was, after the Lord God,
and so I am, as you can well see;
I am as fair as the sun in summer.
And the other fairy gave me far better,
but I do not want to tell just now
what the fairies told me and gave me.
Rightful emperor,” said the noble Oberon,
“so help me God, the king of majesty,
who greatly loves right and faith and loyalty;
that is why I love Huon, the young knight,
for he is a worthy man, and I have well proved it.”
With this word, he has called Huon.
“Friend,” he said, “now quickly, get up:
and above all Duke Naimes the bearded.
The court breaks up; they stay there no longer;
King Oberon has called Huon.
“Huon,” he said, “listen to me:
I command you, as you hold me dear,
when three years have passed, you will come to Monmur,
and you will have all my kingdom,
and with that you will have my dignity.
Know for certain that I can well give it to you,
for I tell you in very truth
that so it was ordained for me at my birth
that I may give it to whomever I wish;
and I love you in good loyalty,
so I will give you all my dignity.
You will wear a crown of gold on your head,
and you will give your inheritances to Gériaume,
for he has well deserved them, in God’s name:
he has served you with his heart and without falseness,
and he has endured many hardships for you.
He is a very worthy man and of great loyalty;
he ought to fare the better for it, so may God save me.”
“Sire,” said Huon, “you have spoken very well;
I will give them to him, since you command it.”
Oberon said: “Friend, now listen to me:
I no longer wish to remain in the world;
I want to go up there to paradise,
for our Lord has truly sent me word,
and I will do his will.
My seat is at his right side;
I no longer wish to stay in fairyland.
Do not let what I tell you slip into forgetting,
and I forbid you, on pain of having your limbs cut off,
and on the faith you owe me,
ever again to quarrel with the king;

“Sire,” said Huon, “I will do all your will in this.”
King Oberon has asked leave to go;
he embraced Charlemagne the noble,
on parting he pleads with him for young Huon,
kissed Huon, and then has turned away.
He goes back to Monmur, his city,
taking with him all his rich company of barons.
